items.stem: Why was the post-Maurya era also known as the era of reorganisation?
items.answer:  It was called the ‘era of reorganisation’ because the unified Maurya Empire broke apart, leading to the emergence of many new, competing kingdoms. Existing regions were reorganized under new rulers, and foreign invaders also established kingdoms, reshaping the political map of the subcontinent.

items.stem: Write a note on the Sangam literature in 150 words.
items.answer:  Sangam literature is the earliest known body of Tamil literature, composed between 300 BCE and 300 CE. It flourished under the patronage of the Chera, Chola, and Pandya kingdoms in South India. The term “Sangam” refers to assemblies or academies of poets and scholars held in Madurai, where these works were compiled. Sangam literature is primarily secular and includes poems, ethical texts, and heroic tales written in classical Tamil. The major works are grouped into two categories : Akam (love and personal life) and Puram (war, politics, and public life). Notable texts include the Ettuthokai (Eight Anthologies) and Pattuppattu (Ten Idylls). These poems offer rich insights into the social structure, economy, warfare, and cultural life of early Tamil society. Sangam literature is also significant for its lyrical beauty, realism, and detailed portrayal of nature and human emotions, making it a valuable source for understanding ancient South Indian history and culture. NODIA

items.stem: Which rulers mentioned in this chapter included their mother’s name in their title, and why did they do so?
items.answer:  The Satavahana rulers, like Gautamiputra Satakarni (son of Gautami Balashri), often included their mother’s name. While the succession was patrilineal, using the mother’s name likely signified the high status and influence of queens and women in the royal family during that period.

items.stem: Write a note of 250 words about one kingdom from this chapter that you find interesting. Explain why you chose it. After presenting your note in class, find out what kingdoms have been the most selected by your classmates.
items.answer:  One of the most fascinating kingdoms from this chapter is the Maurya Empire, which I chose because of its remarkable scale, administrative brilliance, and the legacy of Emperor Ashoka. Founded by Chandragupta Maurya around 321 BCE with the guidance of Chanakya (Kautilya), the Maurya Empire was the first empire to unify most of the Indian subcontinent under a single rule. What makes the Maurya Empire particularly interesting is its well-organized administrative system. It had a centralized government with provincial divisions, a vast bureaucracy, and a structured taxation system. The empire also maintained a strong standing army and had an efficient spy network, as described in Kautilya’s Arthashastra. However, it was under Ashoka the Great (ruled c. 268–232 BCE) that the empire reached its peak. After witnessing the bloodshed of the Kalinga War, Ashoka embraced Buddhism and focused on dhamma (moral rule), promoting non-violence, tolerance, and welfare. He spread these ideals through inscriptions and pillars across the empire. His efforts to govern through ethical principles and promote harmony set him apart as one of history’s earliest proponents of state-led moral governance. I chose the Maurya Empire because of its unique blend of military strength, administrative innovation, and philosophical depth. It shows how leadership can evolve from conquest to compassion, making it not just a political but also a moral turning point in Indian history.

items.stem: You have read about the architectural developments of the post-Maurya era. Take an outline of the Indian subcontinent and mark the approximate locations of some of the ancient structures mentioned in this chapter.
What does the term ‘Age of Reorganisation’ primarily refer to in the context of post-Maurya Indian history? regions reorganised into new kingdoms

options.label: A
options.text: A period of complete political stability

options.label: B
options.text: The re-establishment of the Mauryan empire

options.label: D
options.text: The decline of all trade and urban life

items.answer:  (C) Existing regions reorganised into new kingdoms The ‘Age of Reorganisation’ describes the period after the Mauryan empire’s decline, where existing regions were restructured into new, often competing, kingdoms, and new political powers emerged across the Indian subcontinent over time.

items.stem: Who is generally accepted as having assassinated the last Maurya emperor around 185 BCE, leading to the empire’s breakup?
items.answer:  (C) Pushyamitra Shunga Historical accounts suggest that Pushyamitra Shunga, the commander-in-chief of the last Maurya emperor, assassinated him around 185 BCE. This event marked the end of the Mauryan dynasty and the beginning of the Shunga dynasty.

items.stem: Why did the northwest region of the Indian subcontinent become weak and exposed to invasions after the Mauryan empire’s decline?

options.label: A
options.text: Due to severe and prolonged natural disasters

options.label: B
options.text: The breakup of a strong central Mauryan

options.label: C
options.text: Local rulers invited foreign powers to help

options.label: D
options.text: Trade routes in the region were closed

items.answer:  (B) The breakup of a strong central Mauryan The disintegration of the powerful Mauryan empire, which had maintained control over the vast northwest, led to a power vacuum. This made the region vulnerable to invasions from groups outside the subcontinent.

items.stem: What is a ‘matrimonial alliance’ in the context of ancient kingdoms? envoys marriage

items.answer:  (C) An alliance arranged through a strategic marriage A matrimonial alliance refers to a political or strategic partnership between two royal families or kingdoms that is solidified through a marriage, often involving a king offering his daughter to a neighboring royal family.

items.stem: Pushyamitra Shunga, founder of the Shunga dynasty, performed which Vedic ritual to establish himself as a powerful ruler?
items.answer:  (B) Ashvamedha yajna Pushyamitra Shunga conducted the ashvamedha yajna, an elaborate Vedic horse sacrifice ritual. This ceremony was traditionally performed by powerful kings to assert their sovereignty and imperial ambitions over neighboring territories. NODIA

items.stem: The Shunga period witnessed a revival of Vedic rituals and practices. What does this suggest about the cultural trends of that time?

options.label: A
options.text: A complete rejection of all other beliefs

options.label: B
options.text: The exclusive patronage of Buddhist institutions

options.label: C
options.text: A renewed emphasis on older traditions

options.label: D
options.text: The widespread adoption of foreign customs

items.answer:  (C) A renewed emphasis on older traditions The revival of Vedic rituals during the Shunga period indicates a renewed focus and patronage of older indigenous religious and cultural traditions, although other schools of thought, like Buddhism, also continued to exist.

items.stem: The Yoga Sutras, a foundational text of Yoga philosophy, were compiled by _____ during the Shunga period.
items.answer:  (B) Patanjali Patanjali is credited with compiling the Yoga Sutras, an important classical text that systematically outlines the philosophy and practice of Yoga. This compilation is believed to have occurred during the Shunga period.

items.stem: The Bharhut Stupa, known for its beautifully carved railings depicting stories from Buddha’s life, was significantly enhanced during which dynasty’s rule?
items.answer:  (C) The Shunga dynasty While the original Bharhut Stupa might have been built earlier, possibly during Ashoka’s time, the Shungas are known for adding elaborately carved railings and reliefs, which are prime examples of early Buddhist narrative art.

items.stem: The Hathigumpha inscription, recording King Kharavela’s accomplishments, is written in which ancient script?
items.answer:  (B) Brahmi script The Hathigumpha inscription, a significant historical record detailing the reign of King Kharavela of Kalinga, is inscribed in the Brahmi script, one of ancient India’s most important writing systems for all.

items.stem: King Kharavela’s claim in the Hathigumpha inscription that he was a ‘respector of every sect and repairer of every temple’ highlights what important Indian ethos? patronage

options.label: D

items.answer:  (C) A tradition of religious tolerance and patronage Kharavela’s assertion reflects a long-standing Indian ethos where rulers often extended their respect and support to various religious sects and schools of thought, even if they personally adhered to a specific faith.

items.stem: A group of historians is studying an ancient South Indian literary corpus known for its poetic expressions of personal emotions like love, and societal values like heroism. This literature, the oldest in the region, defined an entire era. Which literary tradition are they likely studying for this work?
items.answer:  (C) Sangam literature Sangam literature, the oldest body of Tamil literature, is renowned for its anthologies of poems that beautifully articulate themes of love (akam) and heroism/public life (puram), defining the Sangam Age in South Indian history.

items.stem: The epic Silappadikaram, telling the story of Kannagi and Kovalan, takes the reader through the ancient kingdoms of the Cholas, Pandyas, and the _____.
items.answer:  (C) Cheras The narrative of Silappadikaram unfolds across the three major ancient Tamil kingdoms : the Chola kingdom (Puhar), the Pandya kingdom (Madurai), and finally the Chera kingdom, where Kannagi is deified.

items.stem: The Kallanai, or Grand Anicut, an ancient water diversion system on the Kaveri River, is attributed to which Chola king?
items.answer:  (C) Karikala Chola The construction of the Kallanai (Grand Anicut), one of the world’s oldest water-diversion structures still in use, is traditionally attributed to the early Chola king Karikala, around the 2nd century CE.

items.stem: The term ‘Keralaputra’ (sons of Kerala) was often used to refer to which ancient South Indian dynasty?
items.answer:  (C) The Cheras The Cheras, who ruled over parts of present- day Kerala and western Tamil Nadu, were also known by the epithet ‘Keralaputra’, signifying their strong association with the Kerala region in ancient times.

An Indo-Greek ambassador adopting Indian religious devotion (to Vasudeva) and erecting a pillar with an Indian philosophical message demonstrates the blending of cultures.

items.stem: The Shaka Samvat, adopted as the Indian National Calendar, is how many years behind the Gregorian calendar for most of the year?
items.answer:  (B) 78 years behind The Shaka Samvat (Shaka Era) calendar begins 78 years after the start of the Gregorian calendar (Common Era). Therefore, to convert a Shaka year to a Gregorian year, one generally adds 78.

items.stem: The ‘Gandhara School of Art’, which flourished under rulers like the Kushanas, is known for its fusion of which two major artistic styles?
items.answer:  (C) Indian and Greek styles The Gandhara School of Art is celebrated for its distinctive style that blended Indian themes, particularly Buddhist iconography, with Greco- Roman artistic techniques and aesthetic elements, resulting in unique sculptural forms.

items.stem: Which of the “crowned kings” of the Sangam Age ruled with their capital at Madurai and were known for their pearl fisheries?
items.answer:  (C) The Pandyas The Pandyas, one of the three “crowned kings” (Muvendar) of the Sangam Age, had their capital at Madurai. They were renowned for their rich pearl fisheries and extensive trade in pearls with other regions.

items.answer:  (C) Kharavela - Kalinga (Eastern India, Odisha) King Kharavela was a powerful ruler of the Chedi dynasty in Kalinga, which corresponds to modern-day Odisha in eastern India. Kanishka ruled the Kushan empire in the north, Karikala was a Chola king, and Pushyamitra Shunga ruled in northern/central India.

items.stem: A trader from Rome arrives in a South Indian port during the 1st century CE, seeking to buy pearls, spices, and fine textiles. Which ancient Tamil kingdoms would this trader most likely be interacting with for these goods at that time?

options.label: A
options.text: The Mauryas and the Guptas mainly

options.label: B
options.text: The Shungas and the Kanvas only

items.answer:  (C) The Cholas, Cheras, or Pandyas The Cholas, Cheras, and Pandyas were the prominent Tamil kingdoms in South India during this period. They had flourishing maritime trade with the Roman Empire, exporting goods like pearls, spices, and textiles.

items.stem: Which of the following was NOT a major characteristic of the “Age of Reorganisation” in post-Mauryan India? one

options.label: A
options.text: The emergence of many new smaller kingdoms

options.label: B
options.text: A period of complete political unity under

options.label: C
options.text: Invasions from groups outside the subcontinent

options.label: D
options.text: Significant developments in art and literature

items.answer:  (B) A period of complete political unity under one The “Age of Reorganisation” was marked by the fragmentation of the Mauryan empire and the rise of multiple competing kingdoms and foreign invasions. It was a period of political flux, not complete unity under a single empire.

items.stem: The Heliodorus pillar inscription, an important archaeological find, is located near which present- day city in Madhya Pradesh?
items.answer:  (B) Vidisha The Heliodorus pillar, famous for its inscription by an Indo-Greek ambassador dedicated to Vasudeva, stands near the ancient city of Vidisha (Besnagar) in Madhya Pradesh, providing crucial evidence of Indo-Greek cultural interaction.

items.stem: What does “Sangam” refer to in the context of ancient South Indian literature and history?

options.label: A
options.text: A type of fortified royal palace

options.label: B
options.text: An assembly or academy of poets, scholars

options.label: C
options.text: A specific style of temple architecture

options.label: D
options.text: A dynasty of kings who ruled in south

items.answer:  (B) An assembly or academy of poets, scholars “Sangam” in this context refers to ancient assemblies or academies of Tamil poets and scholars, traditionally believed to have flourished in Madurai under the patronage of the Pandya kings, producing a rich body of literature.

items.stem: How did the Indo-Greeks initially establish their presence in northwestern India after Alexander’s campaign? Downloaded from www.pdf.tube

options.label: A
options.text: They were invited by local rulers to form

options.label: B
options.text: They migrated peacefully as traders and

options.label: C
options.text: Satraps left by Alexander established domains

options.label: D
options.text: They were remnants of the earlier Mauryan

items.answer:  (C) Satraps left by Alexander established domains After Alexander the Great retreated from India, the Greek governors (satraps) he left behind in the conquered northwestern territories gradually established their own independent or semi- independent kingdoms, which came to be known as Indo-Greek kingdoms.

items.stem: The Hathigumpha inscription at Udayagiri caves details the year-by-year accomplishments of King _____ of Kalinga.
items.answer:  (C) Kharavela The Hathigumpha (Elephant Cave) inscription is a detailed prasasti (eulogy) that chronicles the military victories, public works, and religious patronage of King Kharavela, a powerful ruler of the Chedi dynasty of Kalinga.

items.stem: The discovery of Roman coins in South Indian archaeological sites primarily indicates what about the region during that period? Rome

options.label: A
options.text: Roman military conquest of South India

options.label: C
options.text: Migration of Roman artisans to South India

options.label: D
options.text: Adoption of Roman currency as official one

items.answer:  (B) Extensive maritime trade relations with Rome The presence of Roman coins in South India is strong evidence of active and substantial maritime trade between the Tamil kingdoms (Cholas, Cheras, Pandyas) and the Roman Empire, with Indian goods being exchanged for Roman currency.

items.stem: An art historian examines a sculpture depicting a Bodhisattva. The figure has a blend of Indian features and distinct Greco-Roman elements in its hairstyle, robe drapery, and realistic portrayal. The material is grey-black schist. This artwork most likely originated from the :
items.answer:  (C) Gandhara school of art region The combination of Buddhist themes with Greco- Roman artistic influences (realistic anatomy, drapery) and the use of grey-black schist stone are defining characteristics of the Gandhara school of art, which flourished in northwestern India.

items.stem: Which ancient Indian dynasty is INCORRECTLY paired with its significant contribution or characteristic? numerals Buddhism styles

options.label: A
options.text: Shungas - Patronage of Bharhut Stupa art

options.label: D
options.text: Kushanas - Fusion of Indian and Greek art

items.answer:  (C) Chedis (Kharavela) - Strict adherence to Buddhism King Kharavela of the Chedi dynasty was a devout follower of Jainism, not Buddhism, although his Hathigumpha inscription states he respected all sects. The other pairings correctly reflect contributions or characteristics.

items.stem: Assertion (A) : The Mathura school of art developed a distinct Indian style, using red sandstone. Reason (R) : The Mathura art style was completely isolated and showed no influence from other contemporary Indian artistic traditions. explanation of A. correct explanation of A.

options.label: A
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct

options.label: B
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the

options.label: C
options.text: A is true, but R is false

options.label: D
options.text: A is false, but R is true

items.answer:  (C) A is true, but R is false The Mathura school is known for its indigenous Indian style and use of red sandstone. However, like any art form, it would have interacted with and been influenced by other contemporary artistic trends within India, rather than being completely isolated. NODIA CH 06: The Age of Reorganisation

items.stem: The Kushanas controlled parts of the Silk Route, enhancing trade. Which of the above statements is/are correct for that?
items.answer:  (A) 1 and 3 only Indo-Greek coins are a primary source for their history and often show rulers. The Kushanas did control parts of the Silk Route. The Indo-Greeks were among the first significant foreign groups to establish kingdoms after Mauryan decline, followed by Shakas.

items.stem: The term “Silk Route” refers to a network of ancient trade routes that primarily connected China with the _____ world.
items.answer:  (C) Mediterranean The Silk Route was an extensive network of trade routes that connected East Asia, particularly China, with the Mediterranean world, passing through Central Asia, Persia, and India, facilitating the exchange of goods like silk, spices, and ideas.

items.stem: What is meant by a “headless statue,” such as the famous one of King Kanishka? head

options.label: A
options.text: A statue that was intentionally made without

options.label: B
options.text: A statue whose head has been broken off

options.label: C
options.text: A symbolic representation of a ruler’s power

options.label: D
options.text: A statue buried underground up to its neck

items.answer:  (B) A statue whose head has been broken off A “headless statue” refers to a sculpture from which the head is missing, usually due to damage or breakage over time. The famous statue of Kanishka found at Mathura is an example, with only the body remaining.

items.stem: The Sangam literary works are primarily associated with which ancient language of South India?
items.answer:  (D) Tamil language Sangam literature represents the earliest corpus of extant literature in the Tamil language. These classical works, comprising poems and epics, are foundational to Tamil literary tradition and South Indian history.

items.stem: The cultural confluence during the “Age of Reorganisation,” involving both indigenous dynasties and foreign invaders, led to what significant outcome in art and culture? traditions influences

options.label: A
options.text: The complete disappearance of all Indian

options.label: B
options.text: The creation of new styles with blended

options.label: C
options.text: The strict separation of foreign and local art

options.label: D
options.text: A decline in all forms of artistic creation

items.answer:  (B) The creation of new styles with blended influences This period of interaction between indigenous Indian cultures and foreign groups like the Indo- Greeks and Kushanas resulted in a rich cultural confluence. This led to the development of new artistic styles (like Gandhara art) that blended diverse influences.

items.stem: Which ancient South Indian kingdom is correctly paired with its traditional royal emblem often seen on its coins or artifacts?
items.answer:  (C) Pandyas - Fish symbol used The Pandyas of ancient South India typically used the fish (often a pair of fish) as their royal emblem, which is frequently found on their coins and inscriptions. Cheras had the bow and arrow, Cholas the tiger.

items.stem: A team of archaeologists excavates an ancient port city in South India and finds Roman pottery, amphorae, and coins alongside local artifacts dating to the early centuries CE. This discovery strongly suggests that the city was involved in :

options.label: A
options.text: Isolating itself from all external influences

options.label: B
options.text: Primarily overland trade with Northern India

options.label: C
options.text: Active maritime trade with Roman Empire

options.label: D
options.text: Conflicts with invading Roman naval forces

items.answer:  (C) Active maritime trade with Roman Empire The presence of Roman artifacts like pottery and coins in a South Indian port city from this period is compelling evidence of significant maritime trade relations between South India and the Roman Empire.

items.stem: Which of these was NOT a prominent dynasty ruling parts of India during the “Age of Reorganisation” (approx. 2nd century BCE - 3rd century CE)?
items.answer:  (C) The Mauryas The “Age of Reorganisation” specifically refers to the period after the decline of the Maurya Empire. The Satavahanas, Kushanas, and Indo- Greeks were among the prominent dynasties that rose to power during this subsequent era.

items.stem: The Grand Anicut (Kallanai Dam) on the Kaveri River is one of the oldest water-regulation structures in the world still in use. Its construction is attributed to which ancient dynasty?
items.answer:  (C) The Chola Dynasty The construction of the Grand Anicut, an engineering marvel of ancient India, is traditionally attributed to the early Chola king Karikala, dating back to around the 2nd century CE, showcasing advanced irrigation techniques.

items.stem: What does the term ‘assimilation’ mean in the context of cultural interaction between different groups? other another mixing

options.label: A
options.text: The complete rejection of one culture by

options.label: B
options.text: The process by which one group absorbs

options.label: C
options.text: The peaceful coexistence without any real

options.label: D
options.text: The deliberate destruction of cultural heritage

items.answer:  (B) The process by which one group absorbs another Cultural assimilation refers to the process whereby a minority group or culture comes to resemble a dominant group or assume the values, behaviors, and beliefs of another group, often involving a blending of traditions.

items.stem: How did the geographical focus of the Shunga empire differ from that of the Chera kingdom? south northwest

options.label: A
options.text: Shungas were north/central; Cheras were in

options.label: B
options.text: Shungas were far south; Cheras were

options.label: C
options.text: Both were primarily located in eastern India

options.label: D
options.text: Shungas were west coast; Cheras east coast

items.answer:  (A) Shungas were north/central; Cheras were in south NODIA CH 06: The Age of Reorganisation The Shunga empire primarily controlled parts of northern and central India after the Mauryas. The Chera kingdom, on the other hand, was a prominent power in the southern part of the subcontinent, mainly in present-day Kerala and parts of Tamil Nadu.

items.stem: The period of the Shungas saw the flourishing of Sanskrit literature, including the compilation of the Yoga Sutras by _____.
items.answer:  (C) Patanjali Patanjali, the great sage and grammarian, is credited with compiling the Yoga Sutras, a foundational text of Yoga philosophy, during the Shunga period, which also witnessed a broader resurgence in Sanskrit literature.

items.stem: The presence of multiple dynasties ruling different parts of the Indian subcontinent simultaneously during the “Age of Reorganisation” indicates what about the overall political landscape? powers

options.label: A
options.text: A unified empire under a single supreme

options.label: B
options.text: A fragmented political scene with regional

options.label: C
options.text: The absence of any organized state system

items.answer:  (B) A fragmented political scene with regional The simultaneous existence of several dynasties like the Shungas, Satavahanas, Kushanas, and southern kingdoms points to a politically fragmented subcontinent where various regional powers coexisted, competed, and sometimes formed alliances.

items.stem: A museum displays a gold coin from ancient India. One side shows a king in foreign attire, and the other shows a Hindu deity like Shiva with his bull Nandi. Such a coin is characteristic of rulers who : religion deals

options.label: A
options.text: Strictly prohibited the practice of local

options.label: B
options.text: Adopted or showed respect for Indian deities

options.label: C
options.text: Used coinage only for international trade

options.label: D
options.text: Were isolated from all Indian cultural ways

items.answer:  (B) Adopted or showed respect for Indian deities Invading rulers or foreign dynasties, like the Kushanas, often depicted Indian deities on their coinage alongside their own portraits or symbols. This indicated a degree of cultural assimilation and respect for local religious beliefs.

items.stem: Which of these ancient Indian literary works is INCORRECTLY paired with its general theme or content? values justice Sutras - Techniques of state administration work

options.label: A
options.text: Sangam Poetry - Love, heroism, and social

items.answer:  (C) Yoga Sutras - Techniques of state administration Patanjali’s Yoga Sutras are a classical text on the philosophy and practice of Yoga, focusing on meditation, ethics, and spiritual discipline, not state administration. The other pairings are generally correct for those.

items.stem: Assertion (A) : The Mathura School of Art primarily used grey-black schist stone for its sculptures and showed strong Greco-Roman influence. Reason (R) : The Gandhara School of Art, in contrast, used red sandstone and developed a more distinct indigenous Indian artistic style. explanation of A. correct explanation of A.

options.label: A
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct

options.label: B
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the

options.label: C
options.text: A is true, but R is false

options.label: D
options.text: Both A and R are false

items.answer:  (D) Both A and R are false Both statements are incorrect. The Mathura school used red sandstone and had a distinct Indian style. The Gandhara school used grey- black schist and showed Greco-Roman influence. The descriptions are swapped here.

items.stem: The Cheras exclusively traded with Central Asian empires over land. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
items.answer:  (A) 1 and 2 only The Cholas, Cheras, and Pandyas are indeed referred to as the “Muvendar” (Three Crowned Kings). Sangam literature is the earliest extant Tamil literature. The Cheras were known for maritime trade, especially with Rome.

items.stem: The Indo-Greek ambassador Heliodorus erected a famous pillar near Vidisha, dedicating it to the deity _____, whom he praised as ‘god of gods’.
items.answer:  (C) Vasudeva The Heliodorus pillar inscription explicitly states that it was erected by Heliodorus, an ambassador of an Indo-Greek king, in honor of Vasudeva (a form of Vishnu/Krishna), whom he revered as the “god of gods” (devadeva).

items.stem: What does “Shaka Samvat” refer to?

options.label: A
options.text: A style of Shaka period temple architecture

options.label: B
options.text: A calendar era initiated during Shaka rule

options.label: C
options.text: A specific type of coin issued by Shakas

options.label: D
options.text: A philosophical text written by Shaka one

items.answer:  (B) A calendar era initiated during Shaka rule The Shaka Samvat (Shaka Era) is a historical calendar era that is believed to have been initiated during the rule of the Shakas (Indo-Scythians) in India. It is still used as the Indian National Calendar.

items.stem: The flourishing of Sanskrit literature, including the final compilation of epics like the Mahabharata and Ramayana, during this “Age of Reorganisation” suggests what about the cultural environment? activity

options.label: A
options.text: A complete decline in all forms of learning

options.label: B
options.text: A period of significant literary and cultural

options.label: C
options.text: The exclusive use of Prakrit languages

options.label: D
options.text: A suppression of all epic storytelling forms

items.answer:  (B) A period of significant literary and cultural activity The compilation and flourishing of major Sanskrit literary works, including the great epics, indicates a vibrant cultural and intellectual environment during this period, with continued development and refinement of classical Indian traditions for all. MAT CHING TYPE QUESTION 

items.stem: Who is generally accepted as the last Maurya emperor’s assassin and founder of the Shunga dynasty?
items.answer:  Pushyamitra Shunga.

items.stem: Around what year BCE did the Maurya empire break up?
items.answer:  Around 185 BCE.

items.stem: What term do some scholars use for the post- Maurya period characterized by new competing kingdoms?
items.answer:  Age of reorganisation.

items.stem: What is an alliance arranged through marriage between royal families called?
items.answer:  Matrimonial alliance.

items.stem: Which Vedic ritual, involving a horse, did Pushyamitra Shunga perform to assert power?
items.answer:  Ashvamedha yajna.

items.stem: Which ancient text on Yoga was compiled by Patanjali during the Shunga period?
items.answer:  Yoga Sutras.

items.stem: Name the stupa in Madhya Pradesh known for its railings and reliefs added by the Shungas.
items.answer:  Bharhut Stupa.

items.stem: Which powerful dynasty, sometimes called ‘Andhras’, ruled large parts of the Deccan after the Mauryas?
items.answer:  Satavahanas.

items.stem: Name one famous capital city of the Satavahanas.
items.answer:  Amravati/Pratishthana (Paithan) (any one).

items.stem: What objects often depicted ships, suggesting significant Satavahana maritime trade?
items.answer:  Coins.

items.stem: Name the Satavahana king mentioned who was named after his mother, Gautami Balashri.
items.answer:  Gautamiputra Satakarni.

items.stem: In which caves near Pune were inscriptions found detailing a Satavahana queen’s rituals and donations?
items.answer:  Naneghat Caves. Click Here to Buy book on Amazon CH 06: The Age of Reorganisation

items.stem: Which dynasty rose to prominence in Kalinga after the Mauryas?
items.answer:  Chedi dynasty.

items.stem: Name the main Chedi ruler known from the Hathigumpha inscription.
items.answer:  Kharavela.

items.stem: Near which modern city are the Udayagiri- Khandagiri caves located?
items.answer:  Bhubaneswar.

items.stem: What collective name is given to the oldest Tamil literature from this era?
items.answer:  Sangam literature.

items.stem: What does the word ‘sangam’ (derived from sangha) mean in this context?
items.answer:  Association or assembly (of poets).

items.stem: Name the three ‘crowned kings’ or major kingdoms of the Sangam Age in the South.
items.answer:  Cholas, Cheras, and Pandyas.

items.stem: Which Chola king is credited with building the Kallanai (Grand Anicut)?
items.answer:  Karikala.

items.stem: What other name were the Cheras known by?
items.answer:  Keralaputra (‘sons of Kerala’).

items.stem: What group established kingdoms in Northwest India after Alexander’s satraps?
items.answer:  Indo-Greeks.

items.stem: Which group, also called Indo-Scythians, invaded after the Indo-Greeks?
items.answer:  Shakas.

items.stem: Which calendar system, adopted as India’s National Calendar, originated during the Shaka period?
items.answer:  Shaka Samvat.

items.stem: Which dynasty, originally from Central Asia, established a large empire including North India around the 2nd century CE?
items.answer:  Kushanas.

items.stem: Name the most powerful Kushana ruler, known from a famous headless statue.
items.answer:  Kanishka. SSHORT Answer QUESTIO 

items.stem: Why is the period following the Maurya empire sometimes called the ‘Age of Reorganisation’?
items.answer:  After the large, centralized Maurya empire collapsed, the subcontinent saw existing regions reorganised into numerous smaller, competing kingdoms, alongside invasions, leading to a new political map.

items.stem: Describe the purpose and process of the ashvamedha yajna ritual.
items.answer:  It was a Vedic ritual for rulers to declare supremacy. A special horse wandered freely; territories it crossed unchallenged became part of the king’s empire, while challenging it led to battle.

items.stem: What evidence shows Shunga patronage of art, despite the revival of Vedic practices?
items.answer:  The Shungas added beautifully carved railings and reliefs depicting Buddhist themes (like Jataka tales) to the existing Bharhut Stupa, showcasing their contribution to Buddhist art. NODIA

items.stem: How do Satavahana coins indicate the importance of trade, particularly maritime trade?
items.answer:  Satavahana coins found across wide regions suggest extensive trade. Many coins specifically depict seafaring ships with masts and sails, indicating that maritime trade was a significant part of their economy.

items.stem: Explain the Satavahana tradition of naming rulers like Gautamiputra Satakarni.
items.answer:  Some Satavahana kings followed a matronymic system, taking their mother’s name first (e.g., ‘Gautamiputra’ means ‘son of Gautami’). This possibly signifies the high status or influence of queens or mothers in their society.

items.stem: What does the Hathigumpha inscription tell us about King Kharavela’s rule?
items.answer:  It records his accomplishments year-by-year, including military victories and public welfare works. It also highlights his devotion to Jainism while claiming tolerance and respect for all sects and sages.

items.stem: What is Sangam literature, and why is it important for historians?
items.answer:  Sangam literature is a collection of ancient Tamil poems from assemblies (Sangams) of poets. It’s the oldest South Indian literature, providing valuable insights into the society, culture, values (love, heroism), and kingdoms (Chola, Chera, Pandya) of that era.

items.stem: Briefly narrate the story of Kannagi from the epic Silappadikaram.
items.answer:  Kannagi’s husband Kovalan wrongly executed in Madurai. She proved his innocence with her matching anklet, causing the shocked Pandya king to die. Kannagi’s curse destroyed Madurai by fire before she was deified.

items.stem: What was the significance of the Kallanai (Grand Anicut) built by Karikala Chola?
items.answer:  The Kallanai was an ancient, complex water diversion structure on the Kaveri river. It irrigated large parts of the delta, enabling extensive rice cultivation and making the region highly productive agriculturally.

items.stem: What goods did the Chera kingdom primarily export, and with whom did they trade?
items.answer:  The Cheras exported valuable goods like spices (pepper), timber, ivory, and pearls. They had extensive trade connections, particularly with the distant Roman Empire and West Asia.

items.stem: How did the Indo-Greek kingdoms emerge in Northwest India?
items.answer:  After Alexander the Great retreated, the Greek governors (satraps) he left behind gradually established their own independent kingdoms in the northwestern regions of the subcontinent, becoming known as the Indo-Greeks.

items.stem: Give an example of cultural blending during the Indo-Greek period.
items.answer:  The Heliodorus pillar near Vidisha, erected by an Indo-Greek ambassador, praises the Indian deity Vasudeva. Indo-Greek coins sometimes depicted Indian deities alongside Greek ones, showing cultural interaction and adoption of local beliefs.

items.stem: What is the Shaka Samvat, and how does it relate to the Gregorian calendar?
items.answer:  The Shaka Samvat is a calendar era developed during the rule of the Shakas (Indo-Scythians). It is India’s National Calendar and runs 78 years behind the internationally used Gregorian calendar (mostly).

items.stem: Describe the extent of the Kushana empire at its peak.
items.answer:  The Kushana empire was vast, stretching from parts of Central Asia through present-day Afghanistan and Pakistan into large parts of northern India, controlling important trade routes like the Silk Route. Downloaded from www.pdf.tube CH 06: The Age of Reorganisation

items.stem: What titles did Kushana king Kanishka use, as seen on his statue’s inscription?
items.answer:  The inscription reads ‘maharaja rajadhiraja devaputra kanishka’, meaning ‘The great king, king of kings, son of God, Kanishka’, indicating lofty claims to power and divine connection.

items.stem: How do Kanishka’s coins reflect religious tolerance or patronage?
items.answer:  His coins depicted not only the emperor but also deities from different traditions, notably Buddha (with Greek script label) and the Hindu god Shiva with Nandi, suggesting patronage or acknowledgement of multiple faiths.

items.stem: What was the Silk Route, and why was controlling parts of it important for the Kushanas?
items.answer:  The Silk Route was a network of ancient trade routes connecting China with the West (Mediterranean) via Central Asia. Controlling sections allowed the Kushanas to tax lucrative trade, boosting their economy and influence.

items.stem: Briefly describe the key difference between the Gandhara and Mathura schools of art.
items.answer:  The Gandhara school (NW India), using grey schist, showed strong Greco-Roman influence (realistic anatomy, flowing robes). The Mathura school (Uttar Pradesh), using red sandstone, reflected a more distinct Indian style (fuller figures, Indian deities).

items.stem: What types of deities were commonly depicted by the Mathura school of art?
items.answer:  The Mathura school depicted a wide range of Indian deities, including figures like Kubera (wealth god), Lakshmi, Shiva, Buddha, as well as yakshas and yakshinis (nature spirits).

items.stem: How did art during the Kushana period lay groundwork for later temple architecture?
items.answer:  This era saw increased development of religious art, including representations of deities that looked more human. This focus on depicting gods and creating dedicated religious imagery paved the way for later, more elaborate temple structures.

items.stem: What major Sanskrit epics were likely composed during this ‘Age of Reorganisation’?
items.answer:  This period saw the flourishing of Sanskrit literature, notably including the composition (or compilation into near-final form) of the great epics, the Mahabharata and the Ramayana.

items.stem: What does the inscription made by the goldsmith Kanhadasa on the Pitalkhora yaksha sculpture suggest?
items.answer:  It suggests that artisans during the Satavahana period might have been skilled in multiple crafts, as a goldsmith also crafted a stone sculpture, indicating versatility in professions.

items.stem: What evidence suggests the Satavahana queen who performed Vedic rituals held significant power?
items.answer:  The Naneghat inscriptions detail her performance of major Vedic rituals (like ashvamedha, usually done by kings) and extensive donations, indicating she wielded considerable religious and political authority as a widow queen.

items.stem: Why was maintaining control over border areas important for kingdoms during this period?
items.answer:  Border areas were constantly contested. Controlling them was crucial for defending the kingdom from attacks by neighbouring rivals or foreign invaders, ensuring the core territory remained secure. NODIA CASE BASED QUESTIO 

items.stem: Archaeologists excavate a site identified as a Satavahana trading post on the west coast. They find Roman pottery shards, Satavahana coins depicting ships, local pottery, and remnants of warehouses. Nearby, inscriptions mention donations made by a local traders’ guild (shreni) to a Buddhist monastery. (i) What does the discovery of Roman pottery indicate about this site? (ii) How do the ship coins and warehouse remnants support the idea of a trading post? (iii) Evaluate the role of the traders’ guild and their relationship with Buddhism, based on the inscription.
items.answer:  (i) It indicates direct or indirect trade connections with the Roman Empire, confirming the Satavahanas’ participation in long-distance maritime trade, likely importing Roman goods. (ii) Ship coins signify the importance of sea trade to the Satavahanas. Warehouses suggest the storage of goods received via ships or awaiting export, characteristic of a trading centre. (iii) The guild’s donation suggests economic prosperity and organized activity among traders. Their support for a Buddhist monastery indicates patronage of religion, possibly for social merit or because Buddhism was popular among mercantile communities, highlighting links between trade, wealth, and religious patronage.

items.stem: A Kushana governor in Mathura needs to commission sculptures for a new temple complex intended to appeal to both local Indian worshippers and officials familiar with Greco- Roman aesthetics from the western parts of the empire. (i) Which local school of art, known for using red sandstone, would be primarily involved? (ii) To incorporate Greco-Roman aesthetics, elements from which other art school might be subtly blended in? (iii) Evaluate the governor’s likely aim in commissioning art that blends styles.
items.answer:  (i) The Mathura school of art, known for using local red sandstone and depicting Indian deities, would be primarily involved. (ii) Elements might be borrowed or adapted from the Gandhara school of art, which was known for its fusion of Indian themes with Greco- Roman stylistic features. (iii) The aim is likely political and cultural integration. By blending styles, the governor acknowledges both local traditions and the broader cultural influences within the diverse Kushana empire, fostering goodwill and reflecting the era’s syncretism.

items.stem: A ruler in the post-Maurya period wants to declare his supremacy over neighbouring territories without engaging in costly wars immediately. He decides to perform a significant Vedic ritual. (i) Which Vedic ritual would be suitable for this purpose? (ii) Explain how performing this ritual asserts the ruler’s power symbolically. (iii) What risk did the ruler take by performing this ritual?
items.answer:  (i) The ashvamedha yajna (horse sacrifice) would be suitable for declaring supremacy over neighbours. (ii) The unchallenged journey of the sacrificial horse through neighbouring territories symbolically represents those rulers’ acceptance of the sponsoring king’s overlordship. Successfully completing the ritual proclaims his paramount status. (iii) The main risk was that a neighbouring ruler might challenge the horse’s passage, forcing the sponsoring king into a battle to prove his claimed supremacy, potentially leading to the war he initially sought to avoid.

items.stem: Analyse the importance of inscriptions (like Hathigumpha, Naneghat, Ashokan edicts revisited) and coins as historical sources for this period.
items.answer:  Inscriptions provide direct accounts of rulers’ achievements, policies, religious beliefs, and administrative actions (Kharavela, Satavahana queen, Ashoka). Coins reveal rulers’ names, titles, timelines, economic conditions (metal used), trade links (find spots), religious affiliations (deities depicted), and artistic styles, offering crucial data where literary sources are scarce.

items.stem: Based on the examples of Satavahana queens and the mention of women fighters against Alexander, evaluate the possible role and status of women during this period.
items.answer:  Evidence suggests varied roles. Satavahana queens (Gautami Balashri, Naneghat queen) wielded considerable influence, performing rituals and issuing inscriptions. The mention of women fighting implies participation beyond domestic spheres in some contexts. However, this limited evidence doesn’t allow generalizations but hints at potentially significant, though diverse, roles for women.

items.stem: Compare the factors contributing to the decline of the Maurya Empire and the Satavahana Empire. Are there common themes?
items.answer:  Both empires faced issues inherent in managing large territories. Weak central control after powerful rulers (Ashoka’s successors, later Satavahanas) allowed regional powers to assert independence. Economic factors (strain of administration/campaigns, potentially economic decline for Satavahanas) also played a role. Thus, weakened central authority and economic pressures seem common themes.

items.stem: How does the story of Kannagi in Silappadikaram reflect societal values concerning justice and a ruler’s dharma?
items.answer:  The story emphasizes the ideal of swift, accurate justice as a ruler’s primary duty (dharma). The Pandya king’s death from shock upon realizing his unjust execution of Kovalan underscores the immense moral weight of a king’s judgement. Kannagi’s transformation and destructive power symbolize the severe consequences when justice fails.

items.stem: Analyse the title ‘Devaputra’ (Son of God) used by Kushana king Kanishka. What might be the purpose of such a title?
items.answer:  This title, likely borrowed from Chinese or other imperial traditions, aimed to elevate the king’s status above ordinary mortals. It suggests a claim to divine mandate or connection, legitimizing his rule, enhancing his authority over diverse subjects, and placing him on par with great emperors of other cultures.

items.stem: Discuss the interplay between warfare and diplomacy (like matrimonial alliances) as methods used by kingdoms to gain power during this period.
items.answer:  Kingdoms used both. Warfare (Pushyamitra vs neighbours, Karikala vs Cheras/Pandyas) aimed at direct conquest and asserting supremacy. Diplomacy, especially matrimonial alliances, was used to build peaceful relationships, secure borders, gain allies against common enemies, and consolidate power without the cost and risk of war. Both were tools in the constant competition.

items.stem: “The ‘Age of Reorganisation’ set the stage for future empires by fostering regional powers and cultural identities.” Evaluate this statement.
items.answer:  This period saw the rise of strong regional kingdoms (Satavahanas, Kushanas, Southern kingdoms) with distinct cultural identities (art, literature, trade specializations). While politically fragmented compared to the Mauryas, these developments created powerful regional bases and rich cultural traditions that would influence and be incorporated into subsequent larger empires like the Guptas. items.stem: Analyse the reasons why the period after the Mauryan decline (c. 185 BCE - 300 CE) is termed the ‘Age of Reorganisation’.
items.answer:  The term reflects profound changes. The unified Maurya empire fragmented, leading to political reorganisation with new regional kingdoms (Shungas, Satavahanas, Chedis, Southern kingdoms) emerging and competing. Simultaneously, foreign invasions (Indo-Greeks, Shakas, Kushanas) led to further political shifts and significant cultural reorganisation through assimilation and interaction.

items.stem: Compare the political strategies used by rulers like Pushyamitra Shunga and Kharavela to assert their authority.
items.answer:  Pushyamitra Shunga used the traditional Vedic ritual, the ashvamedha yajna, signifying military dominance and royal power legitimised through ancient rites. Kharavela, while also highlighting military victories in his inscription, emphasized his adherence to Jain principles and his role as a benevolent ruler respecting all sects, asserting authority through both might and righteousness/ tolerance.

items.stem: “The Satavahana period demonstrates a balance between indigenous traditions and external connections.” Analyse this statement using evidence related to trade and culture.
items.answer:  Satavahanas promoted indigenous culture (Vedic rituals, Prakrit language, local art styles) and unique social customs (matronymics). Simultaneously, they engaged extensively in external trade, reaching the Roman Empire, indicated by coins depicting ships and Roman goods found in their territory. This shows a blend of internal development and outward-looking engagement.

items.stem: Evaluate the significance of the Sangam Age for the history and culture of South India.
items.answer:  The Sangam Age was foundational for South Indian culture. Its literature (oldest Tamil works) provides invaluable insights into the society, values, and politics of the Chola, Chera, and Pandya kingdoms. It established Tamil as a major literary language and documented a distinct cultural identity, influencing regional heritage profoundly.

items.stem: Analyse the process of cultural assimilation as seen during the periods of Indo-Greek and Kushana rule in Northwest India.
items.answer:  Invading groups (Indo-Greeks, Kushanas) brought their own traditions but were significantly influenced by local Indian culture. This resulted in syncretism : rulers adopted Indian religions (Vaishnavism, Buddhism, Shaivism) depicted on coins; art styles fused Greco-Roman and Indian elements (Gandhara); even foreign ambassadors adopted local faiths (Heliodorus). Invaders gradually integrated into the Indian cultural fabric.

items.stem: Explain the development and characteristics of the Gandhara and Mathura schools of art. What do they reveal about the cultural dynamics of the time?
items.answer:  Gandhara art (NW) blended Indian themes with Greco-Roman styles (realism, drapery), using grey schist. Mathura art (North India) used red sandstone, developing a more indigenous Indian aesthetic (fuller figures, local deities). Their coexistence and distinct styles reveal intense cultural interaction alongside strong local artistic traditions during the Kushana period.

items.stem: How did control over sections of the Silk Route benefit the Kushana Empire economically and culturally?
items.answer:  Economically, controlling Silk Route segments allowed Kushanas to tax the lucrative trade between East (China) and West (Rome), generating significant revenue. Culturally, it placed them at a crossroads, facilitating the exchange of goods, ideas, religions (like Buddhism spreading to Central Asia/China), and artistic styles, enriching their diverse empire.
